ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This intensive longitudinal cohort study (approved by the University of Kentucky Institutional Review Board; written informed consent) was conducted 2019-2024 at the University of Kentucky (Lexington).
table.header: Design and participants.

table.text: Participants provided evening symptom ratings (ADHD, affect, pain) and morning saliva (E2, P4, and luteinizing hormone) at home for up to about 70 days (unselected start phase; about 2 cycles).
table.header: Design and participants.

table.text: Eligible participants were 18-35 years, naturally cycling monthly, not pregnant, breastfeeding, or using hormones, and endorsed clinically significant ADHD symptoms on the Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale (BAARS-IV).
table.header: Design and participants.

table.text: Values for robustly cyclical participants are in-sample estimates in participants selected for exceeding their own null, so they are upper bounds; in 2-fold crossvalidation, median cyclic R² among robustly cyclical participants whose two halves could both be evaluated was 17% (inattention) and 12% (hyperactivity-impulsivity; eMethods 3).
table.header: Keywords: menstrual cycle; ovarian hormones; estradiol; progesterone; ADHD; executive function.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants provided evening symptom ratings (ADHD, affect, pain) and morning saliva (E2, P4, and luteinizing hormone) at home for up to about 70 days (unselected start phase; about 2 cycles).

> Eligible participants were 18-35 years, naturally cycling monthly, not pregnant, breastfeeding, or using hormones, and endorsed clinically significant ADHD symptoms on the Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale (BAARS-IV).

> Values for robustly cyclical participants are in-sample estimates in participants selected for exceeding their own null, so they are upper bounds; in 2-fold crossvalidation, median cyclic R² among robustly cyclical participants whose two halves could both be evaluated was 17% (inattention) and 12% (hyperactivity-impulsivity; eMethods 3).

Ethics approval statement:

> This intensive longitudinal cohort study (approved by the University of Kentucky Institutional Review Board; written informed consent) was conducted 2019-2024 at the University of Kentucky (Lexington).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Analyses used R 4.5 with per-outcome distributional families; we report both uncorrected P and Benjamini-Hochberg (27) q values (eMethods 2). Person-level analyses used only days anchored by observed menses onset (≥10 days, ≥1 per cycle quarter; 1 exception, eMethods 1); population models used every day with PACTS cycle time. Population effects were estimated with generalized additive mixed models on PACTS cycle time, with a personlevel random cyclic factor-smooth (eMethods 2). Person-specific generalized additive models (cyclic cubic spline) estimated each patient's cycle curve; cyclic R² was defined as the share of a participant's day-to-day variance explained by the cycle, and amplitude was the curve's peakto-trough difference. A participant was classified as robustly cyclical if cyclic R² or amplitude exceeded the 95th percentile of a within-person permutation null distribution (5,000 time shuffles of the participant's own days; eMethods 3), with P values computed per Phipson and Smyth (28). The simulated false-positive rate of the cyclic R² criterion was 4.7%; power to detect a true cyclic R² of 0.3 was 59% overall and 91% with at least 30 rated days, so prevalence estimates are likely conservative (eMethods 3). Smoothing mixture models identified latent curve-shape classes matching the DASH-MC hypothesized risk windows (eMethods 4). Phase-elevation scores were calculated as the mean elevation of a participant's own curve, relative to their cycle mean and in units of person-SD, within 3 a priori DASH-MC hormone-timed windows over PACTS time (luteal; menstrual, from menses to early follicular phase; peri-ovulatory). Mixed models related each outcome to daily E2 and P4 levels and the interaction (eMethods 5; eTable 4). Working-memory models are described in eMethods 6. Cycle-level PMDD diagnosis used the standardized Carolina Premenstrual Assessment Scoring System (4) (C-PASS; eMethods 7). Medication was examined as a moderator of cyclic change (eMethods 8).

table.header: Correlates of robust cyclicity.
table.expanded: Robust ADHD cyclicity was more common in patients with informant-confirmed ADHD (exploratory; 69% vs 36%; odds ratio [OR], 3.9; 95% CI, 1.4-11.2; P = .004; q = .11 across 30 characteristics; eTable 6).

table.formatted: Inattention cyclic R² was higher with informant-confirmed ADHD (d = 0.54; 95% CI, 0.10-0.98; P = .02; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">2</ref>).
table.header: Correlates of robust cyclicity.
table.expanded: Inattention cyclic R² was higher with informant-confirmed ADHD (d = 0.54; 95% CI, 0.10-0.98; P = .02; Table 2).

table.header: Working memory, but not inhibition, dipped where a patient's own inattention
table.expanded: In 85 participants (321 in-lab visits), the working-memory deficit (higher = worse) was greater at the cycle positions where the participant's own inattention cycle was high (within-person β = 0.27 per own-SD; 95% CI, 0.02-0.52; P = .03; q = .13; eFigure 2; eTable 8).

table.formatted: Participants with greater menstrual worsening of inattention had poorer working memory just after menses (P = .06; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1D</ref>) and, more strongly, at cycle positions where normative E2 is low (elevation × normative E2, β = -0.11; 95% CI, -0.17 to -0.04; P = .001), a pattern specific to E2 (joint P4 term, P = .95; eMethods 6).

table.header: Cyclical ADHD was not explained by PMDD.
table.expanded: Medication did not account for cyclicity: stimulant users had a flatter sample-average ADHD cycle (P ≤ .004; q = .02; eFigure 3) but were robustly cyclical on either ADHD domain at least as often as non-users (either domain, 63% vs 50%; P = .41), and the cycle did not differ by selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use (eTable 13).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

table.formatted: Among robustly cyclical participants, lower within-person E2 and P4 accompanied worse hyperactivity-impulsivity (P = .004 and P < .001; q ≤ .03; inattention with E2, P = .07; eTable 4), and hormone slopes varied significantly across all participants (random-slope tests, P < .001 for inattention with E2 and P4 and hyperactivity-impulsivity with P4; eMethods 5).
table.header: Cyclical ADHD was not explained by PMDD.

table.formatted: E2 and P4 cycles did not differ detectably between those with and without robust ADHD cyclicity, in shape or level (all P ≥ .39; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. summary_table.ethics_statements: This intensive longitudinal cohort study (approved by the University of Kentucky Institutional Review Board; written informed consent) was conducted 2019-2024 at the University of Kentucky (Lexington).
live_data_statements: Participants provided evening symptom ratings (ADHD, affect, pain) and morning saliva (E2, P4, and luteinizing hormone) at home for up to about 70 days (unselected start phase; about 2 cycles).

Eligible participants were 18-35 years, naturally cycling monthly, not pregnant, breastfeeding, or using hormones, and endorsed clinically significant ADHD symptoms on the Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale (BAARS-IV).

Values for robustly cyclical participants are in-sample estimates in participants selected for exceeding their own null, so they are upper bounds; in 2-fold crossvalidation, median cyclic R² among robustly cyclical participants whose two halves could both be evaluated was 17% (inattention) and 12% (hyperactivity-impulsivity; eMethods 3).
